summary.text: Gram staining is a laboratory method that sorts bacterial species into two large groups, gram-positive and gram-negative.

It works because the groups differ in their cell walls: gram-positive cells have a thick peptidoglycan layer that holds the crystal violet stain, while gram-negative cells have a thinner one that lets it wash out.
Developed by Hans Christian Gram in 1884, it is almost always the first step in identifying a bacterial group and gives results much more quickly than culturing.

facts.value: Danish bacteriologist Hans Christian Gram, in 1884

facts.value: Results come much more quickly than culturing

items.prompt: Under a microscope, a stained sample shows some cells purple and others pink. What explains the pink ones?

options.label: They lost the first dye and then took up the second one
They are dead cells that cannot hold any dye at all
They have the thickest walls, which block every stain
They took up the second dye before the first one

items.explain: Gram-negative cells lose the crystal violet at the decolorizing step, and the counterstain then colours them pink or red.

items.prompt: A lab worker leaves the alcohol rinse on for far too long, well beyond a few seconds. What is the likely result?

options.label: Only gram-negative cells lose their colour
Every cell keeps its purple colour for longer
Cells stain darker because the dye settles in
Even gram-positive cells lose their purple colour

items.explain: The decolorizing step must be timed carefully because crystal violet is removed from both kinds of cell if the agent stays on too long.

items.prompt: Why is an iodine solution added right after the first dye?

options.label: It dyes the cell wall pink so the cell can be seen
It forms a stable complex with the dye so it holds to the wall
It kills the bacteria so they stick to the slide
It dissolves the outer membrane to let the dye out

items.explain: Iodine combines with crystal violet to form large complexes that strengthen the bond between the stain and the cell wall.

items.prompt: A patient may have meningitis and doctors need an early clue before lab growth results return. Why does a Gram stain help?

options.label: It removes the need to ever check the patient again
It works on every microbe, including archaea
It gives results much faster than growing a culture
It names the exact species from one pink cell

items.explain: Gram stains on fluid such as cerebrospinal fluid yield results much more quickly than culturing, which matters for treatment and prognosis.

items.prompt: What was Hans Christian Gram's original aim when he developed his technique?

options.label: To make bacteria easier to see in stained lung tissue
To sort bacteria into gram-positive and gram-negative
To diagnose fungal infections in hospital patients
To kill bacteria on slides before they were studied

items.explain: Gram wanted bacteria to be more visible in stained sections of lung tissue, and he did not at first make the positive and negative distinction.

items.prompt: A researcher tries to sort archaea into gram-positive and gram-negative groups. Why does this work poorly?

options.label: Archaea have no cell walls, so no dye can hold
Their responses vary widely and do not follow their groups
The dyes only work on cells that are fungi
Archaea are too small to show up under a microscope

items.explain: Gram staining is not used to classify archaea because they give widely varying responses that do not follow their phylogenetic groups.

paragraphs.heading: Sorting bacteria in two
paragraphs.text: The Gram stain is a laboratory method that sorts bacterial species into two big groups, called gram-positive and gram-negative. It tells them apart by how their cell walls behave, chemically and physically. It is almost always the first step in identifying a bacterial group, and it can also help diagnose a fungal infection.

paragraphs.heading: Where it came from
paragraphs.text: The method is named after the Danish scientist Hans Christian Gram, who developed it in 1884 while he worked with Carl Friedländer in the morgue of Berlin's city hospital. He was not trying to tell bacteria apart; he wanted to make them easier to see in stained sections of lung tissue. He noticed that some bacterial cells clearly resisted losing their colour. In his short 1884 report he noted that the typhus bacillus did not keep the stain, but at first he did not split bacteria into gram-positive and gram-negative.

paragraphs.heading: The steps
paragraphs.text: First, the primary stain, crystal violet, goes onto a heat-fixed smear of bacteria. Heat fixing kills some bacteria, but its main job is to stick them to the slide so they do not rinse off. Next comes Lugol's iodine, which forms a stable complex with the crystal violet and acts as a trapping agent that keeps the colour in the cell. Then a decolorizer such as alcohol or acetone is added. Last, a counterstain, usually safranin, gives decolorized cells a pink or red colour.

paragraphs.heading: Why the colours differ
paragraphs.text: Gram-positive cells have a thick, multilayered peptidoglycan wall. Ethanol dehydrates them, and the large crystal violet–iodine complexes get trapped inside, so they stay purple. Gram-negative cells have a thinner peptidoglycan layer. The decolorizer strips off their outer membrane, leaving that layer exposed, and the stain complexes wash away along with the membrane. Timing is critical: if the decolorizer stays on too long, a matter of seconds, both kinds lose the stain.

paragraphs.heading: Pink or purple
paragraphs.text: Both kinds of cell take up the counterstain. On gram-positive cells it cannot be seen, because the darker crystal violet hides it. Gram-negative cells, having lost their purple, are stained pink or red, commonly by safranin or fuchsine.

paragraphs.heading: Use in medicine
paragraphs.text: Gram stains are run on body fluid or biopsy samples when infection is suspected. They give results much more quickly than culturing, which matters most when an infection would change a patient's treatment and prognosis, as with cerebrospinal fluid in meningitis or synovial fluid in septic arthritis. The method has limits: some bacteria cannot be classified clearly and fall into gram-variable or gram-indeterminate groups. Archaea are not sorted this way, because their responses vary too widely and do not follow their family groups.
